statement: In children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD who were taking stimulant medicine and still took more than an hour to fall asleep (on average, or on at least 30% of nights) after a sleep-routine programme (a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in a Vancouver hospital ADHD programme, 19 children analysed, sponsored by the company that made the melatonin; Weiss et al., 2006), melatonin (study conditions in the study card) compared with placebo is associated with falling asleep about 16 minutes sooner on parents' sleep diaries (46.4 against 62.1 minutes; effect size 0.6) and sooner on wrist activity monitors, and with about 15 minutes more sleep on the diaries but not on the monitors. Clinicians' overall ratings of improvement and parents' ratings of ADHD symptoms did not differ between melatonin and placebo; side effects were mild or moderate and were reported about as often with placebo (20% of all reported side effects during melatonin, 23% during placebo). The trial analysed fewer children than its own power calculation required, its statistics imply more children than the 19 it reports, and children's sleep improved over time whatever they took (a significant period effect). Whether melatonin helps without a sleep routine, in children not taking stimulants, or over months under blinded conditions is not known. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Children with ADHD whose medicine kept them awake took melatonin on some nights and a dummy pill on others, without knowing which. With melatonin they fell asleep about 16 minutes sooner. Doctors did not see a bigger overall improvement with melatonin than with the dummy pill, and side effects were mild and as common with the dummy pill. It was one small study, paid for by the company that made the melatonin.
population: Children aged 6 to 14 (91% boys) with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine whose time to fall asleep stayed over an hour after a sleep-hygiene programme, in a hospital ADHD programme
exposure: Pharmaceutical-grade melatonin made by the sponsor (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo, in a randomized crossover with each child as his or her own control
outcome: Time to fall asleep and total sleep (parent diaries, actigraphy), clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms, adverse events
magnitude: Diary sleep-onset latency 46.4 (SD 26.4) against 62.1 (SD 26.6) minutes, t(20) = −3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6; actigraph t(18) = −4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13; actigraph total sleep, clinician ratings and ADHD ratings not different; 20% against 23% of all adverse events.

evidence.locator: Method › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Procedures (p. 514); Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
evidence.extracted: Children aged 6 to 14 on stable stimulant medicine with sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on parents' diaries; those still above 60 minutes (on average, or on at least 30% of nights) after sleep hygiene were randomized by the pharmacy in blocks of four to melatonin and placebo in a crossover with placebo washouts; of 23 eligible, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, and 19 were analysed per protocol.

evidence.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Diary sleep-onset latency was 46.4 minutes (SD 26.4) on melatonin and 62.1 (SD 26.6) on placebo, t(20) = −3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6, with a significant period effect, t(20) = −2.20, and no carryover; actigraph latency was also shorter, t(18) = −4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep was 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13.

evidence.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 3rd paragraph; Safety
evidence.extracted: Clinician-rated treatment response and ADHD ratings did not differ between melatonin and placebo; adverse events were mild or moderate except one severe migraine, the only study-related event was a rash from the actigraph band, and twenty per cent of all adverse events occurred during melatonin and 23% during placebo.

evidence.locator: Title page footnote (p. 512); Method › Medication and Statistical Analysis (p. 515); Disclosure (p. 518)
evidence.extracted: Sponsored as an investigator-initiated trial by Circa Dia BV, which manufactured the melatonin; the first author disclosed ties with Circa Dia and several makers of ADHD medicines; the study aimed to detect a 30-minute change with 25 children.

risk_of_bias.note: Per-protocol analysis whose degrees of freedom do not match the stated 19 children; a significant period effect; no registration; the product was made by the sponsor.

inconsistency.note: Single study; diaries and monitors agree in direction.

indirectness.note: Worded for children on stimulants whose insomnia persisted after a sleep-hygiene run-in.

imprecision.note: One trial of about 20 children; no confidence interval for the difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single trial.

grade.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover starts high. Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. Status single study.
